intro: The following analysis summarizes the shift‑wise feedback for the SSC CGL 2026 Tier 1 exam held on 7 October 2026. All figures presented are unofficial and based on candidate reports. SSC normally normalises scores across shifts to ensure a fair comparison. The difficulty level was generally described as easy to moderate, with some variation between sections and shifts.

faqs.q: What overall difficulty level was reported for the SSC CGL 2026 Tier 1 exam on 7 October 2026?
faqs.a: Across all three shifts, candidates described the paper as easy to moderate overall. While most reports placed the exam in this range, a few noted that quantitative aptitude varied from easy to hard in certain sections.

faqs.q: How many questions did candidates attempt successfully in each shift of the 7 October 2026 SSC CGL Tier 1 exam?
faqs.a: Shift 1 candidates reported good attempts ranging from 77 to 89 questions. Shift 2 saw attempts between 79 and 84.2 questions. Shift 3 candidates attempted between 70 and 86 questions. These ranges are based on unofficial candidate feedback.

faqs.q: Which sections were considered easiest and which were more challenging on 7 October 2026?
faqs.a: General Awareness and English were generally reported as easy across all shifts. Reasoning was mostly easy, though Shift 2 included many statement‑based items that added complexity. Quantitative Aptitude showed the most variation, ranging from easy to moderate to hard, especially in Shift 2 and Shift 3.

faqs.q: What time‑management concerns were raised by candidates for the 7 October 2026 SSC CGL Tier 1 exam?
faqs.a: Candidates across all shifts mentioned difficulty managing the overall time, with particular emphasis on the new sectional timer introduced in this exam. Many felt the timer added pressure, especially in sections with longer quantitative problems.

faqs.q: How does SSC normalise scores across the three shifts for the 7 October 2026 Tier 1 exam?
faqs.a: SSC applies a statistical normalisation process that adjusts raw scores from each shift to a common scale. This ensures that variations in difficulty or time‑management issues across shifts do not affect the final ranking of candidates.
